en: *Shi Dunlun’s Collected Excerpts from the Treatise*, Volume Sixteen, Part Eleven:

The Stage of That Accomplished through Reflection (5b). Regarding the stage of that accomplished through reflection: "reflection" (*cintā*) refers to deliberation; it is the pervasive mental factor of volition (*manasikāra*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). However, because...
Wisdom that arises from reflection is called "wisdom born of reflection. Here,
we take all dharmas accomplished through reflection as the cause.
Its substance (tattva) is that which pervades the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), serving as the substance of this stage (*bhūmi*).
The text is divided into two parts.
First, the three gates are presented and enumerated.
This will be explained in detail later.
Regarding "purity of intrinsic nature," this clarifies the essence of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Because one attains goodness through discernment,
it is called "purified.
As for the discernment of the objects of knowledge:
One investigates all dharmas that are to be known;
one who investigates dharmas investigates the essential meanings of the prose and verse portions of the Buddha’s sūtras.
"Remaining far removed from all inconceivable states" refers to the objects of reserved explanations (*avyākṛta-vastu*) and the objects of realization belonging to stages not yet attained.
"Being able to thoroughly understand the silent teaching and the great teaching" means [understanding these].
Tai said:
"That which is spoken without having received any transmission is called 'silent speech.
That which is spoken having received a transmission, such as hearing it from the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, is called 'great speech.'"
Jizang said:
"The heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists and various evil doctrines are called 'silent discourse.
The orthodox teachings of the Inner Way and various virtuous doctrines are called 'great discourse.'"

Regarding the phrase "generating only a slight degree of faith and understanding toward the Dharma," this means that the "slight portion of the Dharma" does not refer to a small area of knowledge or understanding already mastered. Rather,
it refers to that which should simply be accepted with faith and understanding, and must not be disparaged.
Regarding those few dharmas already distinguished that should be examined with wisdom:
within the second section on the investigation of the objects of knowledge,
the text is divided into three parts.
First, the general question-and-answer regarding the essence;
second, the specific and abbreviated question-and-answer regarding the essence;
and finally, the detailed explanation according to each point.
The detailed explanation is divided into three parts:
first, the explanation of existent phenomena (*bhāva*);
second, the explanation of non-existent phenomena (*abhāva*).
Subsequently, both [aspects] are explained together.
There are two categories of dharmas.
First, five gates are set forth.
This will be explained in detail later.
Regarding the section on phenomena existing by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the text is divided into three parts.
First is the heading and enumeration.
Next is the specific explanation;
finally, it is concluded that the characteristics of the ultimate (paramārtha) exist.
This refers to the attainment of fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) which is suchness itself;
it is not a non-established characteristic,
yet it possesses the characteristics of formal appearance (nimitta).
That is, the dependent nature exists as a present characteristic;
it exists only in the present time, not in the past or future.
For something to exist as a self-characterized phenomenon (*svalakṣaṇasat*) in the present, it must possess four criteria;
that is to say, all provisional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*) are, in brief, of three types.
First, the conventional designation of aggregation (*samudāya-prajñapti*), such as a jar or a basin;

second, the conventional designation of continuity (*santati-prajñapti*), which establishes a single sentient being across the three times based on the uninterrupted notion that "I am that very same person now";
and third, the conventional designation of state (*avasthā-prajñapti*), referring to non-associated [formations] and the like.
Now, because it is not any of these three, it exists as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
First, regarding "the name being obtainable in this locus":

this refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that realizes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which, although free from names and expressions, [is nonetheless apprehended].
Because names accord with the objects they designate, unlike *tathatā* (suchness),
which does not conform to names, the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) can be distinguished [from the other two].
As for "the two things being obtainable":
This excludes the nature of being grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
because although it has a name, it lacks any substantial entity.
Third, this name is not non-definitive with respect to this object.
This is a designation based on a provisional state;
this name applies solely because of this specific phenomenon,
just as the names "blue" and so forth, as they are perceived, definitely refer to those very objects.
It is not like a fever patient who sees blue as yellow;
when the fever subsides, the designation is no longer fixed.
It is because of such confusion that the name is indeterminate.
Furthermore, it is like when a jar is broken into shards, the name "jar" is immediately discarded;
because it is impermanent, its application is not fixed.
Fourth, this name follows after the object without obstruction.

This means that names such as "form" and so forth—whether in an aggregate or in a dispersed state—are said to follow and persist constantly; they do not function like the name "jar," which persists when things are gathered together but ceases once they are separated.
By implication, this means that [the characteristic] functions unimpededly with respect to this entity;
this specifically excludes the conventional designation of an aggregate.
"Existing as a present characteristic" means:
This excludes the provisional existence of a continuum (*saṃtāna-prajñapti*).
Only that which, having already arisen in the present, serves as the cause for the future and the effect of the past,
is a phenomenon existing by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇasat*).
The text concerning common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) also has three parts:
the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Regarding the common characteristics of categories:
Although the five aggregates (*skandha*) differ in their essential natures, they share the common meaning of "accumulation" (*caya*); thus, they are collectively termed "aggregates.
The aggregate serves as a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the common characteristic of accomplishing what is to be done:
Jingyun: Although there are distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the outflowing and non-outflowing,
in terms of the principle of their resulting fruits, they are identical and are both termed the "single type of common characteristic."
Master Ji said:
This refers to the three types of action and the six consciousnesses;
although their essential natures differ, those that are wholesome and associated with outflows are the same.
All experience the fruit of affection;
this is what is called the "common characteristic of what is produced" (*kṛtaka-sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Such categories as these constitute the common characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), namely, that they are impermanent (*anitya*).
According to this passage, the contemplation of impermanence alone is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because it is a contemplation of a generic characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states:
This is because it is taught that direct perception (pratyakṣa) apprehends only objects of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, that treatise states that the five consciousnesses, the ālayavijñāna, and the mind in a state of distraction perceive objects as their own specific characteristics;
this constitutes direct perception.
If the mind within consciousness is concentrated, even when it takes conditioned phenomena as its object and contemplates them as impermanent,
it individually and specifically realizes the impermanence inherent in the very substance of each conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, all direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) have specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects.
The Master Śīlabhadra said:
"Just as one contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent through the four stages of the roots of goodness,
there arises a single aspect of impermanence encompassing all five aggregates, which should be contemplated as manifesting within the mind."
Just as a single thread binds together many flowers,
so too do the five aggregates share a single characteristic of impermanence.
This is not a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If, as in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as impermanent, then five aspects of impermanence will appear before the mind.

Because this single contemplative mind possesses five distinct modes of understanding, it separately realizes the impermanence of the five aggregates; these are also objects of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇaviṣaya*).
A commentator from the West explains:
Just as in the Hīnayāna, the path of seeing contemplates only the true suchness manifested by impermanence as the ultimate specific characteristic;
therefore, it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If the distracted mind takes common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object, it does not know specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It is like seeing the smoke of a fire from a distance and thereby knowing that there is fire.
Because one does not know the intrinsic nature of that fire's heat,
nor knows what kind of fire it is— whether it be grass-fire, dung-fire, or the like—
one explains this within the context of phenomena that exist as conventional designations.
The text is divided into four parts:
first, a general summary of the questions and answers as a heading;
second, the questions and answers that enumerate the names.
Third, the detailed explanation;
fourth, the summary and establishment.
Regarding the discourse on the correspondence of the possessor and the possessed:

To speak of "provisional existence by way of states" refers to those who have distanced themselves from discursive talk of "this" and "that"; to speak of "provisional existence by way of aggregation" refers to [the conventional designation of a collection].
This refers to the description of the gate of a house and so forth.
Jing says:
"By means of this, these discourses—concerning the roundness of a stone, a drop of oil, or a flame of fire—are also said to be conventionally existent as aggregations."
If one speaks of a "fluttering drum," this is a designation for a conventional wind; likewise, what is called a "wind with dust" is also a conventional existence formed by an aggregation.
To manifest that [conventional reality] through that [designation], we speak of things such as "Buddhadatta," "Guṇamitra," or "clothing."
It is also said that [the collection] exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*). Jiji says:
"To manifest this by means of this."
By means of this object, the full range of things is revealed within this very object.
As for "revealing that by means of that," it refers to revealing one distinct object by means of another distinct object.
To be "distant from this and that" means to seek the former two as being like the door of a house;
by this it is shown that everything from the solidity of the earth-element up to the motion of the wind-element functions within the locus of reality (*vastu-sthāna*).
The flames of burning and so forth all function within the characteristics of the conventional.
"Burning" (huǐ) is a specific name for conventional fire,
because that which blazes intensely is called "burning."
By means of that, one reveals that within it:
sentient beings such as Buddhadatta are conventional designations of persons,
while food and drink are conventional designations of phenomena.
It is devoid of this, that, or the middle;
it has doors and so forth,
yet its main gate is small.
It is not that this [gate] is fully exhaustive in manifesting this essence;
nor is it that the gate exists separately from the house and its facade;
nor is it that one thing manifests another.
Therefore, these are both negations.
Regarding the "ten of one hundred" and the "three of ten tens," a question is asked:
Why is it not said that it is one-tenth or two-tenths?
The explanation is:
this is stated according to what is manifest.

Regarding the statement that "the conventional designations established by the multitude consist of six types," this refers here to consciousness and the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) as answers to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This is intended to demonstrate that common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which are provisional phenomena, do not exist apart from substantial phenomena (*dravyadharma*).
In this regard, the specific self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each individual object of apprehension are real entities (*dravyasat*).
The six kinds of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the objects of apprehension are conventional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*).

By superimposing these self-characteristics, one gives rise to verbal expressions; such conceptualized states of appearance and intrinsic nature are called "conventional designations" (*saṃvṛti-prajñapti-vyavahāra*), such as "pot," "bowl," and so forth.
Therefore, the term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) refers to a conceptual superimposition; it does not mean that real characteristics exist.
This is because, with respect to each of the six transformed objects, one superimposes upon them their own essence as if it were a true intrinsic nature.
Although the objective aspects (nimitta) apprehended by the specifically determined objects (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) and other mental factors may also be conventionally designated as such,
these six types are not mentioned for other objects because they necessarily pervade all objects.
The discourse arising from the conventional designations (*prajñapti*) of all people must rely upon these six aspects.
This does not mean that these six characteristics are necessarily merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

Rather, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, attention (*manasikāra*) is able to apprehend the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of an object, while the other mental factors (*caitasika*) apprehend its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In this context, it is stated that [mind] takes both types of objects as its sphere.
Alternatively, since this passage merely cites the general object of the apprehending [mind], it says that "attention takes what is to be apprehended and gives rise to consciousness.

Otherwise, it would contradict treatises such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which state that because the mind grasps the object in a general sense, it is called "mind," yet because it also grasps it in a specific sense, it is also called a "mental factor" (*caitta*).
However, the sixty-fifth [treatise] explains one type of the conventional:
if there is a phenomenon that depends upon other things for its designation of intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
For example, the self (*ātman*) is designated in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*).
One provisionally designates "form" and so forth based on the phenomena characterized by form and so forth;
one establishes "dwellings" and so forth based on the five sense objects and so forth;
and one establishes "birth" and so forth based on the phenomena characterized by the aggregates.
Up to the point where space is conventionally established as non-functioning in dependence upon various forms, and so forth;
the Abhidharmasamuccaya and other treatises may speak of two kinds of conventionalities:
namely, that which depends on the objects of conceptualization and verbal expression, or that which depends on these [very factors].
Regarding other objects of perception,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of the three types of designation (*prajñapti*):
namely, designation by name (*nāma-prajñapti*), designation by experience (*upādāna-prajñapti*), and designation by phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*).
The Vijñaptimātra school also speaks of three kinds of conventional designations (prajñapti):
namely, those based on aggregation, continuity, and states.
The Tattvasiddhi-śāstra speaks of four kinds of conventional designations.
That is to say: the conventional designation based on causes,
the conventional designation based on mutual dependence, and the conventional designation based on continuity.
Conditionally established designations (*prajñapti*).
In the one hundredth chapter of this treatise, it is stated that there are six types of designations, namely:
the designation of aggregation (*samudāya-prajñapti*).
The causality is provisional;
the fruit is provisional;
that which is practiced is provisional.
The provisional [designation] of states and the provisional [designation] of dependence; herein,
as well as in the eighteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it is further stated that there are six [types].
The term "provisional" (jia) refers to the locus from which discourse arises;
this is easily understood.
As for "pavilion" (ting), it refers to a lodging within a district (xian).
"Obstruction" (*rā*) refers to a barrier or wall.
Within the causes of saṃsāra,
"by means of this seed" refers to the seed of karma.
That which is perfumed by this refers to the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-vyañjana*).
That which is assisted by this refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The circulation of those phenomena refers to the arising of birth, aging, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*).
Regarding the cessation within the cause of cessation:
the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three natures that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) is the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
Regarding the cessation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*):
it refers to the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) and the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), which are the abandonments of the afflictions of both the paths of seeing and cultivation.
This cites the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
All paths capable of pacification refer to the untainted (*anāsrava*) paths that pacify and reverse the aforementioned two [types of suffering].
These untainted paths lead to parinirvāṇa, lead toward awakening (*bodhi*), and include their provisions (*sambhāra*) as well as their methods (*upāya*).
"Prospectuous clouds" refers to that which is proximate to the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*) and remote from the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
which can act as an auxiliary companion, can give rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*), and can bring about nirvāṇa.
It is also called the cause of cessation through mutual following. Ji says:
"And those provisions refer to the path of provisions."
Together with its skillful means, it is the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*).
"That which can produce" refers to the seeds that this path can generate;
"that which can accomplish" refers to its ability to bring about the actualization of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) that leads to nirvāṇa.

The *Abhidharmapitaka* (Dharma-skandha-pāda-śāstra), in its ninth chapter, states that the path of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*), the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) are all termed the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
This teaching, however, restricts the causes for returning [to saṃsāra] to only the first four paths.
Furthermore, it is explained that herein both the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory means (*upāya*) are the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
because they constitute the distant and proximate preliminary applications (*prayoga*) prior to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This differs from the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*), where the path capable of pacifying [the afflictions] prior [to the actual abandonment] is itself the uninterrupted path.
Regarding the detailed analysis of its characteristics, which should be understood as they appear in the "Investigation of Cause and Effect" (Causality),
Jing states:
"The stage produced by cultivation (bhāvanā-maya-bhūmi) is designated as the 'fruit of cultivation'."
It may also refer to the subsequent "determination" (*viniścaya*) as the fruit of reflection (*cintā-phala*).
Beiyun states:
"The fruit of reflection is difficult to understand; one should consult the Tripiṭaka Master."
The Tripitaka Master says:
"If one seeks to find it,
one should know its characteristics as they are explained at length in the section on the locus of the fruit (*phalasthāna*) in the treatise."
If [the specific characteristics] are not obtained, one should understand their characteristics by correlating them with the results as explained within the five aspects (*pañca-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the passage in the *Savitarkā-savicārā-bhūmi* that extensively discriminates cause and effect is termed the "result of reflection" (*cintā-phala*).
Regarding the dharmas that serve as causes, it is said that through the aforementioned five causes, one respectively obtains the five fruits.
*Ki* states: "The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, in the section on the *Cintāmayībhūmi*, explains this."
Regarding the "contemplation of cause and effect," this is as already explained in the *Savitarkā Savicārā Bhūmi*.

This refers to the fact that both the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section) and the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Ascertainment) fully elucidate the causes and effects of defilement and purity within the *Savitarkā Savicārā Bhūmi*.
Within the phenomena that are the objects of observation,
if they were devoid of intrinsic nature,
then just as there is no nature of a horse within a cow, [so too would it be for all things].
If it were not of the nature of existence,
then these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of this person would not have the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of that person.
As for the nature of non-conjunction:
it refers to the fact that the three natures of phenomena—
whether tainted or untainted— lack any mutual quality of conjunction with one another.
Regarding "non-existent in the ultimate sense":
because the intrinsic nature described by all conventional expressions does not exist at all when based upon the ultimate truth.
The subsequent text provides a combined explanation of the five kinds of existence and non-existence, which is divided into two parts:
first, a general presentation, followed by a detailed explanation.
Regarding the statement, "The fourth is the characteristic of non-duality," etc.:
The characteristics such as birth and old age are called "differentiated characteristics.
Because they do not possess a separate essence from the phenomena upon which they depend, they are called "non-dual characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics recognized by the characteristics of the phenomenal aspect":
This refers to the discourse on communal designation among the six aforementioned types of discourse.
Regarding the fact that it cannot be declared whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after his parinirvāṇa:
Jingyun: This teaching regards the *nirmāṇakāya* as the Tathāgata;
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, whether he exists or does not exist is ineffable.
The various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceive of the liberated self (ātman) as being called the Tathāgata, asserting that there are three distinct bodies.
Whether it exists or does not exist,
this is a matter that cannot be described.
Furthermore, whereas the former is based on the non-existence of the essence,
this is based on the excellence of the essence;
therefore, it is called "profound."
The five kinds of non-existence should be understood as the opposites of the five kinds of existence, as appropriate.
This concludes the third major section:
the investigation of all phenomena.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation.
Regarding the analytical investigation of the meaning of the sūtras:
According to this treatise, the Sūtra Piṭaka comprises seven of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], excluding these four:
the nidāna, the avadāna, the itivṛttaka, and the jātaka; these four are subsumed within the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Because it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
while the other three [natures] are its attendants;
furthermore, because it excludes the *upadeśa* (treatises), it is subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Among the sevenfold division [of the teachings], excluding the single recitation of verses (*gāthā*) and the chanting of sūtras,
the remaining six divisions of the teaching constitute the meaning of the sūtras (*sūtrārtha*) that is to be investigated and discerned.
Reciting the gāthās alone constitutes the discernment of the meaning of those gāthās;
this is of three kinds.
Verses on the ultimate meaning clarify the principle of selflessness;
verses on the underlying intention explain the intent of those verses,
such as the four intentions and so forth.
Regarding the *Tiyi gāthā* (Verses on the Meaning of Essence),
Jing says:
it refers to elucidating the distinctions among the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
The Master Ki said:
This refers to the meaning of the essential nature within the *gaṇḍavyūha*;
it concerns the *gaṇḍavyūha* from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the citation of the scriptural verses;
second, the detailed explanation thereof.
Among the forty-four verses of the hymn,
Master Tai says:
"In broad outline, they are divided into two."
The first consists of sixteen verses,
which clarify what is observed within the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
The latter consists of thirty-eight verses.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Chapter on Manifesting Purity" and "Able to Contemplate Non-self," Master Bei states:
"The first section consists of eleven verses."
The first clarifies the absence of a self in persons.
Next, there are five verses that clarify the temporal basis for the various distinctions of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
There are twenty-eight verses following this,
which clarify that when one contemplates the aspect of purity as it truly is, one attains purification,
and so forth. Now, based on the determinations of the two masters Jing and Ji, these are divided into twelve sections.
The first nine verses clarify that all phenomena are devoid of sentient beings, a self, and the essence of agency.
The following two verses clarify the nature of affliction for both householders and renunciants: ignorance and craving.
Three verses and five lines clarify the basis,
causes, and temporal phases of the category of affliction (saṃkleśa).
Four verses clarify the specific and general characteristics as well as the contemplation of the two truths.
Verse five contains two stanzas clarifying that the three kinds of triads of phenomena lack the meaning of conjunction.
Verse six contains one stanza clarifying that mental factors of the same nature are associated, not those of different natures, and so forth.
Seven verses clarify the existence and non-existence of persons and phenomena based on the principles of the two truths;
eight verses clarify that the agent and the recipient cannot be described as being either identical or different;
nine verses resolve doubts and objections.
The first fifteen verses clarify the obstacles to liberation from the suffering of accumulated birth and so forth.
The eleventh verse clarifies the ālayavijñāna through the analogy of a pond and its branching streams.
The final seven verses of the twelve [verses] demonstrate the thorough knowledge of liberation and the thorough knowledge of bondage.
Within the first nine verses:
The text is divided into three parts.
The first five verses correctly elucidate non-self and agency.
The subsequent three and a half verses again clarify that phenomena lack agency.
The latter half-verse reveals that phenomena arise from conditions and perish spontaneously.
In the prose commentary, the text is divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation of the verse’s meaning.
This will be explained separately later.
Regarding the antidote to the extremes of superimposition and denial:
to grasp at a self as existing is called superimposition (*samāropa*).
To negate the non-existence of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called "diminution" (apavāda).
This is explained in terms of the common objective sphere of the three vehicles.
It does not mean that phenomena increase or that true suchness (tathatā) ceases.
In the separate commentary,
if explained according to the meaning, it consists of twelve sections.
Thus, this half-verse refutes the self as conceptualized through distinct meanings.
Regarding the statement "the self as distinct from the aggregates is refuted;
all phenomena are likewise without function," etc.,
this refutes the self that is identical to the aggregates.
"Since neither the aggregates nor the self exist at all," this reveals that by not grasping even subtle and manifold selves, one is able to counteract [the view of self].
Jing says:
That is to say, by understanding that there are only the twelve links of existence— the phenomena that flow through the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—
one does not grasp at a truly existent self; thus,
one eliminates the grasping at a sovereign or controller.
Jizang says:
By teaching various subtle dharmas such as the aggregates (skandhas), one is able to counteract the grasping at a sovereign master and so forth;
for [the opponent] does not rely on a single body but instead clings to the existence of many subtle, real selves.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Since the self must, like the aggregates, be neither permanent nor unitary,
if it did not exist, how could one establish the distinctions between internal and external, or the attainment [of results], and so forth?"
Next, there are six [questions]. What are they?
All of them follow the preceding by raising a subsequent inquiry.
The intent of this question is to ask: "If the self does not exist, how can the internal and external be established?"
The second question asks:
"If all things are empty, how can there be one who contemplates emptiness and the object of emptiness that is contemplated?
The third question says:
Since both the object and the subject of observation are empty, how can there be any distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones?

Jing further explains that this also refutes the Śrāvaka-Vātsīputrīya school’s conception of a self-nature (*ātman*) and refutes the misconceptions of ordinary beings who likewise conceive of a self; all such views are inversions.
The fourth question asks:
"If ordinary beings and sages do not exist, how can there be the distinction between the teacher and the taught, or between self and other?
The fifth question asks:
If there were neither a teacher nor those to be taught, how could there be one who is defiled or one who is purified?

To follow worldly affairs to some extent and to likewise engage in coarse and inferior practices while being called "one who has abandoned much desire," and to receive the virtues of *dhūta* (ascetic purification) for the sake of becoming tranquil and free from afflictions—
this is called the cause of training for the purity of abandoning hindrances.
Regarding the statement, "In order to sustain the life-force for the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya),

As for the phrase, "because the benefits obtained further bring forth further benefits," it means that by virtue of the gains received, one subsequently attracts even more gain.
Having attained this, one should not disparage it;
for by disparaging what has been attained, one may instead bring about much greater loss.
As for the five types of evil views:
These are the five afflictions of gain.
In the verse concerning not accepting offerings of faith,
"not being attached to gain and honor" is the general meaning.
Not adhering to wrong views is the second line;

They accept the offerings of the faithful in vain,

Regarding "familiarizing oneself with bedding and seating that accord with meditative concentration":

Therefore, one is subsequently able to give rise to tranquil concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

through firm diligence (*drḍhavīrya*) and heroic abandonment (*vīryotsāha*), one abandons the two evils and cultivates the two virtues.
Regarding the phrase "because one generates desire for all categories of virtue," this explains the lines in the verse concerning "generating desire" and "not increasing evil.
It refers to one who feels the utmost revulsion toward all sensual desires.

The explanation that there is an absence of desire and aversion for the purpose of cultivating wholesome qualities up to the practice of sleep means that the aforementioned sleep is characterized by functional capacity and mental tranquility.

First, it explains being free from drowsiness and sleep by means of contemplating the pure and sublime signs of light;

When wandering for alms and practicing for the benefit of others, one does not dwell in seclusion; or,

To give rise to thoughts of wonder and apprehension regarding subsequent, increasingly superior states [explains] "longing for the sublime."

This indicates a semblance of doubt, excluding the characteristics of true doubt.

that is, practicing with full completeness.

The bodies of humans and devas are called "grounds" (bhūmi) because they are designated by names;
they are precarious due to the loss of wealth through desire.
Those various desires are like dry bones, for they bring no satisfaction.
That is, he subsequently cites a verse to explain the preceding verse.

Regarding the statement that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed under the three types of verbal objects (*vāgvastu*)," the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The paths of time (*adhvan*),
verbal objects (*vāg-vastu*),

The "three kinds" refer to the paths of the three periods of time.

unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are not so.

Within this same meaning, the "sublime desires" (*kāmaguṇa*) are specifically mentioned as that which should be explained.

Because they understand [the meaning] through the mention of the name "desire," those who do not lift their noses but harbor greed and delusion within are advised:

In the second explanation,
the first verse displays those who await their time regarding sensual desires;
this explains the first line.
Because it must be explained accordingly, it awaits the proper time,
as was previously explained in the first set of four successive turnings regarding those who practice erroneously.
The second line should be explained as "abiding accordingly.

In the second verse, the first half is titled "Renouncing Desire is Reasonable," while the second half is titled "Practicing When Subject to Censure is Unreasonable," as well as "Desiring [to Wait] for the Right Time."
The latter half also demonstrates that desire must depend upon time;
this is because if one wishes to experience [an object], it can only be obtained by waiting for the proper time.
The same applies to the third [case].
This also refers to abandoning pride and seeking the absence of pride.
In the third explanation of the second verse,
the phrase "because of being able to thoroughly understand all desires" explains the first line.
Next, two instances of the word "therefore" (故) explain the second line;
next, three instances of the word "therefore" explain the third line.
This fourth section explains the preceding three verses.
Jingyun says:

In other sūtras, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke to the devas, saying that bhikṣus are unable to proclaim the great meaning of the Tathāgata’s holy teaching, whereas he alone is able to do so.
At that time, the devas conceived feelings of contempt toward the bhikṣus and arrogance toward themselves.
Because the Buddha recited the first three verses for them, the devas attained realization and abandoned their feelings of contempt and arrogance.
Master Ji further explained that when the Buddha recited the first three verses for those devas, they attained realization;
upon hearing the first two verses, they developed a profound revulsion toward all sensual desires,
and upon hearing the third verse, they abandoned their disdainful attitude and severed their arrogance.
Regarding the third section, which consists of five verses explaining attachment (*rāga*),
the first verse poses the question and the subsequent four verses provide the answer.
In the response, the first three are the preliminary (upāya) contemplations,
and the last one is the fundamental (maula) contemplation.
Within the preliminary contemplations:
The first is the contemplation of the objects of loathing;
the second is the contemplation of impurity;
the third consists of three contemplations.
First, suffering; second, non-self; third, the contemplation of the mindfulness of the body.
In the prose commentary, it says:
"If one restrains the sense faculties and does not desire to harm or corrupt the mind..."
The fourth verse of the root text is now explained.
Before explaining that verse,
a preliminary analysis and distinction is provided.
Having understood this, [the text] first explains a portion of the verse concerning those learners who have not yet abandoned desire and greed;
subsequently, it provides the formal commentary on the root verse.

Furthermore, it briefly identifies two types of persons (*pudgala*) within whose continuums these fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of desire and greed can be found, and only then does it proceed to explain the fourth verse.
Among the five causes for the arising of sensual desire,
the second is due to delighting in the pleasures of desire,
and the third is due to grasping at the perception of sentient beings such as men and women.
Fourth, due to being oppressed by intense craving.
The fourth section explains three verses in prose;
the first verse consists of the question posed by a celestial maiden.
The Blessed One answered with the remaining two verses:
"In what way does a bhikṣu dwell much?
Among the three—sorrow, joy, and equanimity—in which feeling does he dwell most?"
The lower answer states that one who abides in equanimity transcends five floods (*ogha*) and shall cross over six;
this refers to the time when one abandons the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
at which point one crosses over the five floods of the faculties (*indriya-ogha*).
When severing the five higher fetters,
one must cross the sixth flood of the mental faculty (*manas*).
How can a practitioner of concentration cross the vast flood of sensual desire when they have not yet obtained the waist-boat?

This question concerns how a trainee (*śaikṣa*) applies the skillful means to sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) before attaining the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

It is like the "waist-boat" used by those crossing the ocean in the world: using a gourd, a leather bag, or some other vessel fashioned into a float, which is placed around the waist and is thus called a waist-boat.
The ocean is a metaphor for birth and death;
the mental consciousness is like the waist;
and wisdom is like a boat. Therefore.
In the response consisting of two verses,
the first verse provides the direct answer,
while the second verse provides the concluding answer.
In the prose commentary (*gadya*), only the latter two verses of the response are explained;
as for the statement "dhyāna is deliberation (*vicāra*) and discernment of the truths (*satya-vicāra*)," this is because of the distinction between the beginning, middle, and end.
If one is attached to the union [of sense objects],
one has not yet attained the superior realm;
if one increases attachment or does not abandon attachment, [the same follows].
That is to say, having already obtained an excellent object,
one does not become attached to it; and regarding an unobtained unpleasant object, one does not [anticipate it].
Regarding "the diminution of craving" and "the distinction of detachment from craving":
this refers to having already encountered unfavorable objects.
Furthermore, what is the distinction regarding how one cultivates the concentration of non-discursive thought (*avitarka-samādhi*) and so forth?
It was previously explained that the cultivation of the concentration without applied thought (*avitarka*) is the expedient for severing the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
This is because, since there are three bodies of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) in the first dhyāna,
joy and equanimity arise, which in turn give rise to delusion and craving.
Because vitarka and so forth have not yet been exhausted, one relies on a meditative concentration free from vitarka and vicāra to cultivate the means for abandonment;
this current distinction is that,
by repeatedly practicing based on the second dhyāna, it is called "well-abandoned" in the same manner as the former.

Furthermore, as previously stated, it is explained that by relying on the hearing and reflection concentrations (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī samādhi*) of the desire realm, one becomes weary of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*); therefore, it is called "concentration without discursive thought" (*avitarka-samādhi*).
This serves as the skillful means for severing the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
By relying on the first dhyāna, one abandons desire and severs the lower fetters.
Now, for the second distinction:
one cultivates the second dhyāna,
which is a meditative absorption free from applied and sustained thought.
"Causing the lower fetters to be distanced is called 'well-severed' as in that [previous] case;
the rest is as explained before."
This refers to the realization of phenomena and liberation, all of which are explained as before.
As the Sūtra says regarding "shame as the axle, the mind as the shaft, and the boat":
shame is like the axle of a chariot, capable of gathering the wheels of goodness and driving the chariot of wisdom to transport one across peril and distress.
The waist-vessel is as described above.
Regarding the fifth section, the three and a half verses on fear,
it is divided into three parts.
The first one and a half verses constitute the request;
the next verse provides the answer;
and the final verse offers praise.
Regarding the ten requisites for sustaining the body,
they are as explained previously in the second fascicle and in the fourteenth section of the eighteenth fascicle, within the verses explaining the meaning of the "body" (kāya).
The first five sections above are concluded.
This fascicle contains the next eight full sections,
along with a small portion of the fourteenth section.
Regarding this first category of interpretation, there are three verses:
the first verse poses the question,
and the latter two verses provide the answer.
There are five questions:
first, encouraging superior rebirth;
second, opening the path to liberation.
Third, from which teacher does one study?
Fourth, in what dharma does one abide while studying?
Fifth, one has no fear of death.
In the response,
the first one and a half verses answer the first two questions,
designating the possession of nine qualities.
Having already become a superior person,
one is able to encourage others toward superior rebirths and open the path to liberation.
The latter half of the verse answers the final three questions.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the Dharma, by means of correctness, by means of restraint,
and by means of guidance," Jing says:
This means that by means of the Buddha-dharma and the King’s righteous dharma, the wicked are suppressed and the good are brought to fulfillment.
Sengtai says:
"Yong has four meanings."
First, by means of the teachings;
second, by explaining the correct causes and effects;
third, by means of the disciplinary rules.
"Fourth, by guiding through the three vehicles.
Ji says: "By means of the Dharma refers to the principle."
That which is correct serves to accord with and benefit;
that which regulates serves as a model;
that which guides serves to exhort and encourage.
Furthermore, "Dharma" refers to the teaching;
"Right" refers to the principle;
and "Regulation" refers to the control exercised through these teachings and principles.
The guide instructs and shows the way; he does not punish with severity or through force.
That which is said to be "due to power" refers to giving (*dāna*).
The "man who exerts effort" refers to truthfulness (*satya*).
The companions are wisdom and equanimity.
As for the phrase "like a spring," it refers to the six bases of contact;
the six bases are like a spring.
Afflictions are like water,
because they issue from a spring;
alternatively, they are comprised within the feeling of equanimity.
Master Ji explained:
"Tranquil acceptance" refers to joy (*prīti*);
that which is "subsumed under feeling" refers to pleasure (*sukha*).
Furthermore, that which gladdens the mind is called "physical ease," and this is subsumed under feeling (*vedanā*);
physical unease is the opposite of this.
There is yet another interpretation.
"Tranquil acceptance" refers to joy and bliss.
"That which is subsumed under feeling" refers to body and mind,
or alternatively, it refers to the seeds of feeling.
The ninth section further explains the "floods" (*ogha*) through five verses, which are divided into two parts.
The first two verses demonstrate how ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and others can gradually transcend the violent floods.
The final three verses clarify that one who has attained the path of culmination forever transcends the violent torrent.
Within the first two verses,
the former poses the question and the latter provides the answer.
In the response, the first phrase clarifies that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) transcend the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) through right faith;
the subsequent three phrases clarify that those in training (*śaikṣa*) transcend the remaining three floods.
The meaning of the four floods is as explained previously in the eighth and ninth fascicles, etc.
Regarding the explanation in the final three verses:
as for the twenty-two bases,
they are explained in detail below in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
Furthermore, it reveals those who can realize the path of the first dwelling;
that is, those who can realize cessation.
This is [the subject] within the four verses on the tenth craving.
The first verse poses the question;
the next verse provides the answer;
and the final verse offers the conclusion.
The final section clarifies the counter-refutation.
Within the commentary, according to the interpretations of the two masters Jing and Ji, it is divided into four sections;
the first explains the initial verse.
"How does it moisten? This introduces the explanation of the second verse.
Regarding the explanation of the third verse, the wording differs.

This refers briefly to the six kinds of distinct desires;
the phrase "or perhaps by manual strength" and so forth is from the *Ki*.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, there are śramaṇas" explains the fourth verse.
Now, this is judged as three parts:
first, the explanation of the initial verse;
second, the explanation of how [the moisture] moistens, which explains the following two verses.
Furthermore, there is a śramaṇa who provides an explanation for the fourth verse:
as for the *nyagrodha* tree,
this tree originally grew from a single seed.
Later, when the branches grow large, they hang down and extend upward;
there are sentient beings who dwell upon them.
Furthermore, birds eat the seeds of the tree and drop them onto the forked branches.
Furthermore, many tree roots grow depending on the branches of a tree;
in this manner, through successive development,
many trees are produced from a single original tree.
Water is called the common condition (*sādhāraṇa-pratyaya*).
Therefore, greed, anger, and so forth all take moistening craving as their common condition,
while their respective seeds serve as their individual conditions (*asādhāraṇa-pratyaya*).
The *māluṅga* creeper refers to a type of climbing vine;
this is a metaphor for the various sensual desires.
The old [translation] calls it the "māluka-fruit.
The six kinds of distinct desires are like forest trees;
because greed can entwine them, it is compared to a creeping vine.
Regarding the two types of distinct bonds (*pṛthagbandhana*) among the various [categories] within the summary of meaning,
the treatise itself explains that they are termed "distinct bonds.
That which gives rise to each respective seed is called the "unshared cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*).
All [these] are called "common conditions" because they are moistened by craving.
Regarding the "method of abandonment" and the "excellence of abandonment," these are found in the fourth verse.
The first half of the verse clarifies that once impermanence has been realized, the non-arising of craving and attachment is called the "expedient means of abandonment.
The second half of the verse clarifies that once one has crossed the torrent, the ultimate absence of regression is called the "supreme benefit of abandonment."
Regarding "whether it be greed, whether it be delight,
or even the category of craving," these refer to the categories of craving and aversion that arise within the six specific desires;
they should be understood as previously explained.
Attachment is the sixth type of discursive thought regarding the five external sense objects.
Regarding the eleventh [topic], "Activity," there are five verses;
the first verse poses the question.
The remaining four verses provide the answer.
In the commentary, the first part explains the preceding verse;
the second part, beginning with "Furthermore, it reveals that the Tathāgata relies on the ultimate truth," explains the first response verse.
By this, the second verse of the response is explained through the categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This then explains the third verse of the response through the category of the various *brāhmaṇas*.
This concludes the fourth verse of the response, which explains that those who have attained meditative absorption (dhyāna) have forever severed all lower [defilements].
If one has not yet abandoned desire,
one exerts effort with vigor, moving the feet and hands, in order to cross over the flood of desire.
It is called "not yet reaching the bottom.
If one has already become free from desire,
it is called "attaining the source and bottom."
Having already severed the fetters of the higher realms, he does not move his hands or feet, yet exerts himself with diligent vigor;
this is called "not [relying on] the various parts of the body.
The twelfth section contains five verses.
Within the first four and a half verses concerning diligent effort,
there are three question-and-answer sequences.
The first three lines constitute one such sequence.
The Buddha clarifies that he has crossed the violent torrent;
the devas address the Buddha by the name "Bhikṣu.
These next two lines constitute the second question and answer.
Having clarified that the Buddha is without grasping and without abiding, and has already crossed the violent torrent,
the following three and a half verses constitute the third question and answer, clarifying the characteristics of the Buddha’s lack of grasping, lack of abiding, and crossing of the violent torrent.
Among these, the first verse poses the question,
while the subsequent two and a half verses provide the answer.
Within the answer, the first one and a half verses set forth the obstacles.
The final verse clarifies this:
"As much as I have exerted myself" explains that the Buddha’s six years of ascetic practice in the past were in vain as a mere exertion.
"In such and such a way, one is inferior.
Because of the loss of wholesome qualities through the practice of asceticism, one is called "inferior.
"In whatever way I am inferior, in that very way I abide."
Knowing that my wholesome qualities have declined and that I have abandoned right practice,
those who dwell thus and are drifting in such a manner go again to the presence of non-Buddhist teachers such as Udraka Rāmaputra; their following and observing [of them] is called "drifting."
In the latter part of the Meiji era,
the Buddha again sat beneath the Bodhi tree and abandoned all forms of unskillful, non-beneficial exertion, which he termed "the relinquishing of toil.
As for the absence of decline, it refers to the increase of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*).
Regarding the detailed explanation of "the inferior [state] of the bright white," this phrase contains two meanings:
because one practices without contentment, one dwells in a state of lack of leisure.
This is the reversal of the aforementioned state of abiding.
Because one does not further seek other teachers of non-Buddhist paths and so forth, but spontaneously attains Buddhahood, there is no drifting.
Regarding this, it should be understood that *jyoti* (light) refers to this.
The summary verse of what has been explained above is a *geya-gāthā*.
The prose section consists of three parts.
First, it mentions "no arising" and "no abiding," referring back to what was previously stated.
Regarding the statement "namely, nirvana, the meditative attainment of cessation, and so forth":
if one refers to nirvana, it is called "without grasping" because it is free from the manifest fetters, and "without dwelling" because it is free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If one refers to the meditative attainment of cessation, it is called "without grasping" because perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased, and "without dwelling" because feeling (*vedanā*) has ceased.
From "The World-Honored One, based on what was previously stated" onwards,
the second section explains the third response.
First, it provides a general explanation of the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) within the verse.
This will be explained separately later.
As for those who do not employ skillful means, this refers to the Nigaṇṭhas who daily consume hemp and wheat as a form of perverse asceticism.
As for the Udraka...
This has the meaning of "fierce and intense.
Formerly he was called Udraka Rāmaputra;
there he cultivated the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
"Āḷāha" means "to encounter";
it is the same as the old term "Ālaṃkāla."
Regarding that meditative concentration on nothingness which he cultivated,
it is shown that the practice of asceticism precedes the practice of ease. Herein,
the four meanings of "abandoning exertion" and so forth are to be explained by correlating them respectively with the four phrases of the sutra text.
That is to say: first, when one subsequently sits upon the seat of enlightenment, there is the relinquishing of exertion;
second, all wholesome dharmas that have been acquired subsequently increase, which is the relinquishing of inferiority.
Once the wholesome dharmas have thus increased, this concludes the third [section], dwelling in equanimity;
since one then becomes free from attachment through such lack of complacency, this concludes the fourth [section], being untainted by equanimity;
hence it is said, "in successive order."

How, furthermore, does one rely on nirvāṇa—which is without reliance and without abiding—to manifest the distinctions? This concludes the third section, which retrospectively explains "without reliance and without abiding" from the first two questions and answers.
First, it is explained with respect to nirvāṇa; subsequently, it is explained with respect to the cessation of perception and feeling.
Those who lack support cross over the manifest fetters; those who lack abiding cross over the latent tendencies.
"Returning to dwell in the causes for birth in the lower stages" means that one again regresses and gives rise to the delusions of the fourth dhyāna.
Because the mind abides in that cause, it becomes fixed and proceeds toward the fruit to be obtained therein; this refers to one who,
at the end of life in the desire realm, is reborn in the fourth dhyāna,
as explained in the Abhidharma.

Is there any noble disciple who, having already abandoned desire for the form realm and attained the meditative concentration of the peaceful liberation of the formless realm, is subsequently reborn in the form realm?
The answer is: Yes.
That is to say, one who has attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and then regressed, is reborn within the form realm.
This refers precisely to that.
The meaning of this verse is that while non-Buddhists possess false exertion and the like,
our Blessed One— who has already abandoned the exertion of saṃsāra and has realized nirvāṇa— is certainly free from it.
If a noble one were subject to regression, they would possess such things as toil;
however, a noble one who does not regress has certainly already abandoned them.
This is found in the thirteenth section, the verse on attaining the meaning.
One and a half verses pose the question;
one and a half verses provide the answer.
"To thoroughly know its beginning" means to know the cause of origination (*samudaya*).
Regarding the lower three [knowledges], which are the thorough knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering,
they should be understood respectively as "well-seeing, well-knowing, well-inspecting,
and well-penetrating" by means of the knowledge of the four truths, beginning with the truth of origination.
Below the section on "All Conditioned Phenomena are Impermanent" in the fourteenth chapter,
there are forty-four verses that explain the treatise,
which is further divided into twenty-seven sections.
It is called "discourse" (vāda) because it elucidates and extols profound principles.
Regarding the commentary on the first verse, the text is divided into four parts;
the first explains the initial general statement.
Because there is that which is not always present and that which is not always absent,
both arising and ceasing are impermanent.
